analysis.one_liner: Ends the insurance industry's antitrust exemption for price fixing and monopolization.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the Senate Judiciary Committee at the end of the 102nd Congress in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1945, a federal law called the McCarran-Ferguson Act has exempted the insurance business from most antitrust rules, meaning insurers could agree on prices or divide up markets without facing the lawsuits and penalties other industries face. This bill would have stripped that protection for the worst practices — fixing prices, splitting up territories or customers, forcing customers to buy products they don't want, and monopolizing markets. It kept the exemption for harmless data-sharing, like insurers pooling historical claims statistics so they can price policies accurately.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and businesses buying auto, home, health, and liability insurance, who would gain the ability to sue insurers that fix prices or divide markets, and could see lower premiums if competition replaced coordinated pricing.

how_it_helps.text: It removes the federal antitrust shield for four practices: price fixing, dividing up territories or customers with competitors, illegally tying one insurance product to another, and monopolizing part of the insurance business.

It preserves the exemption for legitimate shared work — collecting and sharing historical loss data, computing loss development factors, and actuarial services — so insurers could still pool the statistics they need to price policies without restraining competition.
The exemption would also remain for insurance businesses that are fully regulated by state law, leaving state regulators' authority intact.

analysis.who_pays: Insurers that engage in price fixing, market allocation, tying, or monopolization would face antitrust suits and damages, and the industry as a whole would lose a legal protection it has held since 1945.

drawbacks.text: Insurers argue the exemption lets them share claims data and actuarial methods that make pricing more accurate, especially in small markets; the bill tries to answer this by exempting data-sharing and actuarial work, but companies would still bear legal risk deciding where the line falls.
The bill takes effect a year after enactment, giving the industry time to adjust but leaving coordinated pricing practices in place during the delay.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit for consumers is straightforward: the same antitrust rules every other industry lives under would apply to insurance price fixing and monopolization, with a carve-out protecting the legitimate data pooling insurers genuinely need. The main cost falls on insurers exposed to litigation and on any pricing arrangements that break up; the bill is narrowly drawn rather than a full repeal of the exemption, which limits both its benefit and its disruption.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the two-year Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Senator Howard Metzenbaum introduced the bill on February 20, 1991, joined by Senators Simon, Biden, and Kennedy as original cosponsors.
Three additional Democratic senators later cosponsored the bill, for seven Democratic sponsors in all.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the day it was introduced; no further action appears in the record for the rest of the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The insurance industry, which keeps the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption and cannot be sued under federal antitrust law for price fixing, market allocation, tying, or monopolization. Consumers gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Howard Metzenbaum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strip the antitrust exemption for insurance price fixing and monopolization.

for.name: Sens. Simon, Biden, and Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup or reported the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Insurance industry
against.role: Industry protected by the McCarran-Ferguson exemption
against.what_they_did: Has long opposed narrowing the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption, which shields insurers from federal antitrust suits over coordinated pricing; opposition groups were active on this issue during the period.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors were Senate Democrats; no Republican support is recorded, and the bill never advanced beyond committee.

industries.note: The bill would strip the industry's 1945 federal antitrust exemption for price fixing, dividing markets, tying products, and monopolization, exposing insurers to lawsuits and damages. Its interest in keeping the exemption runs against policyholders, who currently have no federal antitrust remedy when insurers coordinate prices.

industries.industry: Insurance rating bureaus and actuarial data-sharing organizations
industries.note: The bill explicitly keeps the antitrust exemption for collecting and sharing historical loss data, computing loss development factors, and actuarial services, so the industry's statistical cooperatives could keep operating as they do today.
